name: GoodUI
tagline: 75 UI ideas and 141 patterns backed by 639 replicated A/B tests
description: GoodUI is Jakub Linowski's library of conversion-oriented UI ideas, each tied to real A/B test evidence instead of opinion. The free layer gives you 75 numbered ideas and the list of 141 patterns grouped by screen (Home & Landing, Content, Product, Checkout, Listing, Thank You, Shopping Cart, Signup, Pricing, Global) and by tag (Form, Headline, Pricing, Popup, Personalization, Layout, Button, Photos, Copy, Interaction, Social Proof). The measured effect sizes, the 639-test database and the 'Leaks' section of spotted experiments sit behind a paid membership. It is for product and growth people who need a defensible reason for a UI decision.
pricing_detail: Solo $72/mo, or $60/mo billed yearly ($720). Team (5 seats) $144/mo, or $120/mo billed yearly ($1440). Expert-Guided $1950/mo billed yearly, includes one A/B test review call per month with Jakub Linowski. 30-day money-back guarantee.
agent_guidance: Reach for GoodUI when you must justify a conversion-affecting change (button copy, form length, pricing layout, popup timing) and 'best practice' is not enough — the free idea pages are plain readable HTML and cite direction of effect. Do not promise a user a specific lift percentage from it: the numbers are paywalled at $60-72/mo per seat and you will only see 'Join to see effect'. Pair it with uxpatterns.dev, which gives the accessible implementation GoodUI never covers.
why_it_matters: It is the only widely-known UI reference that ties each recommendation to replicated experiment data rather than taste, which makes it the sane counterweight to inspiration galleries.

name: Growth.Design
tagline: 53 product UX case studies as comics, plus 106 psychology principles
description: Growth.Design publishes teardowns of real products (Amazon, Netflix, Adobe, Apple, Duolingo and others) as illustrated slide-by-slide comics that take five to ten minutes each, currently 53 case studies. Alongside them sits a library of 106 cognitive biases and psychology principles grouped into Information, Meaning, Time and Memory, with a free cheat sheet download. It is run by Dan Benoni and Louis-Xavier Lavallee and monetised through a free email subscription plus paid product-psychology masterclasses. The audience is product designers and PMs who want the behavioural 'why' behind an interface decision.
pricing_detail: Case studies and the psychology library are free with an email or Google signup; some entries are marked 'Premium Psychology'. Paid masterclasses are sold at /courses/product-psychology (price not shown without signup).
agent_guidance: Use the /psychology index, not the case studies, when you need a named principle to justify an onboarding, paywall or activation decision — it is 106 entries of plain text and it fetches cleanly. The case studies themselves are image comics behind a free-signup gate, but each page ships a 'Text version' transcript inside the HTML, so curl the case-study URL and read that rather than trying to describe the pictures. Cite it as behavioural reasoning, never as measured evidence — for numbers use GoodUI instead.
why_it_matters: It made behavioural psychology legible to product teams, and the 106-principle index is the most usable free mapping of cognitive biases onto concrete interface decisions.
notable_for: text transcript embedded in each case study

name: UX Patterns for Devs
tagline: 92 UX patterns with accessibility rules, an MCP server and llms.txt
description: UX Patterns for Developers documents 92 interface patterns across 11 categories (Forms, Navigation, Data Display, Content Management, User Feedback, Authentication, E-commerce, Media, Social, AI Intelligence, Advanced), each with usage guidance, anti-patterns, accessibility requirements and a decision guide for when not to use it. It is framework-agnostic prose and markup rather than a component package, so the advice applies to React, Vue, Svelte, Angular or vanilla JS. The whole thing is MIT-licensed on GitHub by David Dias, publishes llms.txt, and exposes a hosted MCP server at mcp.uxpatterns.dev with 11 tools including suggest_pattern, review_code and check_accessibility.
install: claude mcp add --transport http ux-patterns https://mcp.uxpatterns.dev
agent_guidance: This is the single most agent-native reference in the reference category: wire up the MCP server and call suggest_pattern before you build a control, get_implementation_checklist while you build, and check_accessibility after. Prefer it over a component library's docs when you need to know whether a combobox should commit on blur or what ARIA a date picker owes you — it gives behaviour and a11y rules, not code you can npm install, so pair it with Radix or shadcn for the actual implementation. Its AI Intelligence category (streaming responses, context window, token counter, model selector) is unusually current and worth reading before you hand-roll a chat UI.
why_it_matters: Almost every UX pattern reference is prose for humans; this one ships an MCP server, llms.txt and an MIT repo, which makes it the rare piece of design knowledge an agent can actually query mid-task.
evidence: https://uxpatterns.dev, https://uxpatterns.dev/en/patterns, https://uxpatterns.dev/en/mcp, GitHub API repos/thedaviddias/ux-patterns-for-developers, repo LICENCE.md (MIT, spelled LICENCE so GitHub reports NOASSERTION)

name: Empty States
tagline: 235 curated screenshots of empty-state UI from real shipped apps
description: Empty States is a single-purpose gallery of interfaces with no data yet: no drafts in Outlook, no likes in Figma Community, no card usage in Monzo, empty Slack, Gmail, Reddit, Feedly and Basecamp screens. It holds 235 captures across four pages, filterable by Latest, Mobile, Desktop, iOS and Android, each on its own permalink with the app name, platform and capture date. It is free, static (Gatsby) and needs no account. The collection skews to 2014-2021 captures and shows no sign of recent additions.
agent_guidance: Reach for this the moment you are writing an empty state and the placeholder copy is about to become 'No items found' — the 235 permalink titles alone ('No drafts in Outlook for Android', 'No bookmarks in Basecamp') are readable text and give you the naming and framing pattern without needing to see the image. It is a static Gatsby site with server-rendered links, so it crawls fine, but the substance is in the screenshots, so you cannot extract copy verbatim without vision. Use it for the one element it covers and go to uxpatterns.dev for the accessibility and structure rules around it.
why_it_matters: Empty states are the screen teams forget and users hit first, and this is still the only decent free archive of how shipped products actually handle them.
notable_for: filter by iOS, Android, mobile, desktop
permalink per screen with app and date

name: Really Good Emails
tagline: 19,000+ curated marketing emails, browsable by category, plus a builder
description: Really Good Emails is the reference archive for email design, with 19,000+ curated emails filed under eight top-level groups — Behavioral, Enhancement, Inaugural, Industry, Miscellaneous, Promotional, Punctual and Seasonal — and roughly 150 subcategories such as Abandoned Cart, Welcome, Post Purchase, Re-engagement and Unsubscribe. Browsing categories works without an account; viewing an email's HTML and exporting it runs through RGE Studio, their freemium email builder. There is no public API, and deeper gallery routes return 403 to non-browser clients. It is aimed at email marketers and designers looking for a proven layout or subject-line approach.
pricing_detail: RGE Studio: Starter free (up to 10 designs, 6 exports per month, landing page builder, custom subdomain). Professional $30/mo, or $25/mo billed annually, includes 1 extra seat and AI writing assistant. Business $160/mo, or $134/mo billed annually. Enterprise custom, with Okta SSO.
agent_guidance: Use it for the taxonomy and for naming, not for scraping: /categories is fetchable and gives you the real vocabulary of lifecycle emails (abandoned cart, post purchase, re-engagement, unsubscribe), which is the fastest way to decide what a transactional email should say. Expect 403s on /gallery and other deep routes from non-browser clients, and expect the actual email HTML to sit behind an RGE Studio account with only 6 exports a month on the free tier — so never promise a user you can pull down a template. If the task is 'build an email in code', take the pattern from here and write the table-based HTML yourself.
why_it_matters: Email is the one surface with no component library and no design system, and this 19,000-email archive is the closest thing the discipline has to a canon.
notable_for: RGE Studio builder with HTML export
evidence: https://reallygoodemails.com, https://reallygoodemails.com/categories, https://reallygoodemails.com/pricing, https://reallygoodemails.com/robots.txt, /gallery returned 302 and WebFetch 403; 19,000+ figure from site-reported total via search
